title: The Mystery of the Polished Notes
markdown:
Little Leo slept with the steady breath of someone who had finished the day properly. Moonlight made a silver puddle on the floor, and the curtain-shadows stretched as if they had somewhere to be. In their cosy haven, Walnut Nutmeg, a hamster who liked things just so, nudged his companion. Clover Buttercup, a bunny of fluff and a sunshine sort of spirit, offered a soft inquisitive huff. They did not need a committee. The world beyond the familiar walls had been leaving them homework.

They left the way seasoned explorers leave: a rustle on the carpet, a barely-there sigh from the garden gate, and then the chestnut woods, which by day were merely trees and by moon were an argument for staying up. The air was crisp, damp soil, pine.

For several nights, neat polite messages had appeared on plump toadstools, each more puzzling than a puzzle had any right to be at that hour. “The dew tasted particularly vigorous this morning.” “A most agreeable shade of lichen, wouldn’t you agree?” The pronouncements were courteous and, to Walnut’s orderly mind, nearly rude in their lack of point. Clover’s curiosity did not require an itch; it simply went, ears first.

Deeper in, a hoot dropped from the leafy heights. Professor Hoot occupied a sturdy branch, amber eyes like two small moons that had opinions. Feathers ruffled into importance.

“A bit ordinary for a nighttime show. Lacking in drama. A theatrical tumble, perhaps, or a well-placed sneeze, for the audience.”

Walnut adjusted spectacles that were more a principle than an object. “We are investigating a mystery, Professor. Not performing.” Whiskers admitted a tremor of impatience.

Clover had already found a better plot: a plump bumblebee, golden against the dark. She squeaked, ears on independent contracts, and chased her own tail until she was a white blur of glee.

Professor Hoot sighed like dry leaves. “Misplaced focus. Thematic incoherence. Two stars. The plot thickens, though not in a way that helps.”

Walnut nudged her. “The notes, Clover.”

They came to a stream that had borrowed the moon and a wooden bridge worn smooth by the passage of countless paws. Tonight the planks wore long shadows from ancient branches that leaned as if gossiping over water. It looked like a forgotten tapestry, moonlight woven with dark. Even Walnut, who treated journeys as lists, stopped. Beauty, inconveniently, had no tick-box. Clover did not chase her tail. For a moment the woods were allowed to be only woods.

On the far side, more notes among moss: fungal hues, the velvety blush of a toadstool, the earthy brown of shelf fungus, a spider’s trap considered as architecture.

Walnut’s whiskers drooped. “Exquisite invitations,” he said, “to events that never happen.”

“Maybe they are practising,” Clover chirped, tail a small flag. “A very important letter, and they want it perfect.”

The trail of parchment — mossy crevices, fallen leaves — led to the gnarled roots of an old oak. In a shaft of moon sat a small grey squirrel, brow furrowed, a minuscule quill, an inkpot from an acorn cap. Tongue at the corner of his mouth: the universal badge of trying too hard.

He looked up. The quill thudded on moss. “Oh. I did not hear anyone.”

“You have been leaving the notes,” Walnut said, not as a prosecution. As a click.

The squirrel — Bartholomew — wrung his paws. Tail down. “Yes. Calligraphy. The lines are so precise. And the mushrooms make excellent desks. The woods are quiet. I did not think anyone would read them. Practice. Little exercises in elegance.”

Clover’s smile arrived without a draft. “They are very nice notes. Neat. Polite. It is lovely to have the observations, even as practice.”

Walnut chuckled, a warm sound he usually kept in a drawer. “We were hunting a conspiracy of squirrels. It was a craftsman.” He tipped his head. “You might teach us the script. Mine is rather functional.”

Bartholomew’s tail hoped. Shyness forgot its appointment. “I should like that. We could find mushrooms with the right texture for ink.”

Dawn put pink on the east as if it, too, were practising. Walnut and Clover scurried home, leaving Bartholomew to his desks. The notes would still appear, probably. They would mean less like a riddle and more like a neighbour learning to write. Leo’s breath, when they slipped in, had not changed. The hamster settled his nest until it was just so. The bunny huffed once, satisfied, and did not chase her tail until morning.
characters: Walnut Nutmeg (hamster who likes things just so), Clover Buttercup (a bunny of fluff and sunshine spirit)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
